transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~45m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jonah Patel (Redwood SE), Leila Park (Redwood Solutions Eng), Carlos Ruiz (CTO, Lakeside), Nina Park (Head of ML), Omar Mahmood (SRE), Sofia Lee (Product)

Summary (auto): Discussed latency p95 targets for fraud scoring use case, concurrency and burst patterns, choices between Hosted/Dedicated/Private, security requirements, and next steps to run token/sec benchmarks.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, I'll hand off to Jonah in a bit for the technical part but wanted to do a quick agenda. We're here to understand your p95 latency targets, concurrency, and whether Hosted, Dedicated or Private makes sense.
[00:12] Carlos: Yeah hi thanks, I'm Carlos. Quick intro from our side, Lakeside does card auth + fraud scoring at checkout, we need near real-time decisions, so p95 is critical. We aim for p95 <= 200ms for short prompts (~40-120 tokens) and under 500ms for richer context flows. That is our target, but open to tradeoffs.
[00:30] Jonah: Got it. Are those numbers end-to-end including network, or just inference?
[00:35] Nina: That's end-to-end from our service to the response (so includes our network hop + Redwood). Typical token lengths are 40 tokens for quick decisions, but we also have contextual checks that go to ~300 tokens occasionally.
[00:50] Maya: Thanks. Also curious about concurrency — what's your typical QPS and peak bursts?
[00:56] Omar: Typical steady is ~150 qps, but we see bursts up to 1k qps during peak shopping windows. Latency SLOs need to hold during those bursts, or we fall back to rules.
[01:10] Leila: Okay. A couple quick clarifying q's: do you plan to stream responses back to clients or return whole completions?
[01:15] Sofia: For the fraud use case, we need whole completions; streaming is less important. For other teams streaming might help but not now.
[01:22] Jonah: Good. So main non-functional reqs: p95 200ms for small prompts, p95 500ms for bigger ones, concurrency 150 steady with 1k burst, whole completions. That informs model size and deployment mode.
[01:30] Carlos: One more constraint: PCI environment and we have strict network egress rules, and prefer Private deployment ideally, but if Dedicated with VPC peering and KMS meets compliance we can consider that.
[01:40] Maya: Understood. We typically see three options: Hosted (fastest to integrate), Dedicated (reserved GPU pools w/ VPC options), Private (on-prem or customer VPC with private control plane). For PCI heavy workloads customers usually pick Dedicated or Private.
[01:53] Nina: Can you run through typical p95 numbers for hosted vs dedicated? Even ballpark on a modern LLM is fine.
[01:58] Jonah: Yeah ballpark: on Hosted with our smallest optimized variants we see p95 around 120-250ms for short 40-token prompts on A100-class infra depending on region and networking; Dedicated with pinned capacity and optimized kernels will reduce variance and can hit 80-180ms p95. Private/on-prem depends heavily on your GPUs and network — you can get sub-100ms if you provision enough GPU VMs and use our runtime optimizations. Those are rough.
[02:25] Carlos: Hmm ok and what about tokens/sec and throughput for the burst? We need to understand token/sec per GPU so we can translate to cluster size.
[02:32] Jonah: For example for a 7B quantized model tuned for throughput, you might see ~1000-1500 tokens/sec per GPU for generation workloads with short context. Bigger models 13B could be 400-800 tokens/sec. The runtime supports batching and automatic prefix/KV caching to improve tokens/sec for repeated prompts.
[02:50] Nina: Do you have a recommended benchmark harness we can run? We want to replicate our mix: 70% 40-token prompts, 25% 120-token, 5% 300-token. Also need to replay real traffic traces.
[03:05] Jonah: Yes we'll share our benchmark harness (python runner + k6 script) and a dataset template. We'll help interpret results — especially p95 and tail latencies under concurrency. We'll also provide a small SDK and streaming config options though you mentioned streaming isn't needed.
[03:20] Omar: On networking: our infra blocks outbound internet by default. If we go Dedicated, can we do VPC peering, or do we need Private?
[03:29] Maya: Dedicated supports VPC peering and egress restrictions; data plane can be inside your VPC with peering and private routing. Private gives you the control plane locally too. If security team requires zero internet egress, Private or on-prem is the way.
[03:40] Carlos: What about keys and encryption — KMS, customer-managed keys?
[03:44] Leila: We support KMS integration and HSM-backed keys for Private deployments. For Dedicated we support bringing your own key (BYOK) with envelope encryption and audit logs. Hosted has managed KMS with audit trails and SOC2 controls.
[03:56] Nina: Do you have SOC2 and ISO certifications?
[03:59] Maya: Yes Redwood is SOC 2 Type II and pursuing ISO 27001; we can share the security pack.
[04:06] Sofia: Great. Back to latency: are those p95s measured at your edge or includes network to cloud region? If we do Dedicated in our VPC region, what's the overhead?
[04:15] Jonah: Our p95 numbers include inference time plus a small request routing overhead. If you use Dedicated and route within the same VPC region, expect a 10-30ms improvement vs Hosted due to less public networking.
[04:28] Carlos: For benchmarking, how should we specify model variants? We're considering a 7B quantized model vs a 13B half-precision; cost vs latency tradeoff is important.
[04:36] Jonah: We'll run both. 7B quantized will be much cheaper and faster for short prompts; 13B will give better quality but higher latency and lower tokens/sec. For fallbacks we can set routing policies to preferentially use 7B but fall back to 13B for harder queries or if quality dips.
[04:52] Nina: Is there built-in A/B or canary rollout support? We have to shift traffic gradually and compare quality metrics.
[04:58] Leila: Yes rollouts and canaries are built into the Console — you can do percent-based routing, track evals, and automatic fallback policies if SLA breaches occur.
[05:08] Omar: Real question: during 1k qps bursts can you keep p95 in target or do we need autoscale reserves?
[05:15] Jonah: With Dedicated we recommend reserved capacity sized for your steady load plus burst buffer and autoscaling. For true 1k instantaneous burst you'd need pre-warmed capacity or a burst pool. Autoscaling helps but there's a warm-up time for large allocations. The platform supports burst capacity that can be throttled by cost; implementation detail: you set a burst policy.
[05:34] Carlos: So action-wise, we want an initial benchmark run on Hosted to get baseline, then a Dedicated pilot where you provision a dedicated pool and we run load tests with our traces.
[05:43] Maya: Sounds good. We'll propose a pilot: 2-week trial with dedicated capacity for a few p95 scenarios and we'll supply the harness. Pricing for Dedicated pilot can be credit-backed.
[05:52] Nina: One more: how do you measure p95 exactly — is it request-completion time including queue/batching delays?
[05:59] Jonah: Yes p95 is end-to-end from request arrival at Redwood's ingress to final token delivered to your client. We report token-level timing and queue times; our Console shows breakdown by model, batching time, kernel time, network egress.
[06:12] Sofia: Great. Are there any known failure modes we should plan for? e.g., KV cache misses or OOMs when we change context lengths?
[06:19] Jonah: Common ones: KV cache thrash when context lengths vary a lot, and large concurrent batches increasing memory pressure causing slower scheduling. We mitigate with dynamic KV eviction and per-model memory profiles. We'll help tune quantization and batching to avoid OOMs.
[06:34] Carlos: Ok moving to compliance: we need audit logs for every inference and token-level billing for cost allocation.
[06:41] Leila: Console exposes token-level cost breakdown and request traces; audit logs are available and can be shipped to your SIEM via syslog/S3.
[06:48] Nina: For the benchmark harness, can you add trace output that shows per-request model selection and latency breakdown so we can correlate with our logs?
[06:55] Jonah: Yes we'll add structured telemetry in the runner and map request IDs to Redwood trace IDs.
[07:01] Carlos: Another question: do you support function/tool calling or structured JSON output? We want deterministic outputs for scoring.
[07:09] Maya: We support structured outputs and tool calling. You can enforce output schema and get confidence scores; we recommend a short evaluation harness to validate structure.
[07:17] Omar: About cost — can you give a rule-of-thumb tokens-per-dollar for 7B quantized on Dedicated vs Hosted?
[07:25] Jonah: That depends on instance type and utilization. Roughly: on Dedicated with good utilization you might see 3-5x cost savings vs Hosted per token because you amortize reserved GPU costs. We'll share detailed cost modeling once we know your traffic.
[07:40] Nina: For the pilot, we'll need a pricing worksheet for dedicated pool sizes: 2, 4, 8 GPUs and e.g. expected tokens/sec and estimated p95.
[07:49] Maya: We'll include that in the pricing packet.
[07:52] Sofia: If we do Private, what's the timeline to get on-prem running? Our infra team expects 6-8 weeks for approval and provisioning.
[07:59] Leila: Private tends to be 6-12 weeks depending on networking approvals. We can do a Dedicated pilot in 2-3 weeks while you process Private.
[08:08] Carlos: OK good. Next steps recap?
[08:11] Maya: Recap: 1) Maya to send pricing + Dedicated options and security docs by Friday 2026-03-06. 2) Jonah to upload benchmark harness and runbook by 2026-03-07. 3) Nina to share sanitized traces by 2026-03-06. 4) Schedule technical deep dive week of 2026-03-09 to kick off benchmark. 5) Provision a small Dedicated pilot for 2 weeks once baseline is agreed.
[08:30] Nina: Sounds right. Any blockers?
[08:32] Omar: Our security team will review SOC2 package, and net egress rules might push us to Private. We'll confirm.
[08:40] Maya: We'll share SOC2 and ISO artifacts and a redacted integration guide specific to PCI workloads.
[08:45] Carlos: Thanks, that was helpful.
[08:48] Jonah: Quick note — when you share traces, include request/response lengths and any correlated labels for fraud severity so we can slice results by query type.
[08:57] Nina: Will do.
[09:00] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the packet and calendar invite for the deep dive.

End transcript.
